name: python-prompt-template
comment: Next Term's own grammar (MIT, like the rest of Next Term): Jinja and Mustache tags inside Python strings, the prompt templates of Haystack, LlamaIndex and LangChain. Docstrings and f-strings are left alone. Raw strings are included: R'…' is a plain raw string, and r'…' (which the Python grammar reads as a regular expression) only gains colour where a regex holds {% … %} or {{ name… }}. Each tag is one match within a line, so a tag split over two lines stays plain: a begin/end rule would run past the string's closing quote, to the end of the file, when a string holds only half a tag, as in '{%s}' % x or split('{%').
injectionSelector: L:string.quoted.single.python - meta.fstring.python, L:string.quoted.multi.python - meta.fstring.python, L:string.quoted.raw.single.python - meta.fstring.python, L:string.quoted.raw.multi.python - meta.fstring.python, L:string.regexp.quoted.single.python - meta.fstring.python, L:string.regexp.quoted.multi.python - meta.fstring.python

raw.comment: {% raw %}…{% endraw %}: what is between is literal text.

expression.comment: {{ name }}, {{ doc.content | upper }}, {{ (a or b) }}. Only a name, ( or [ may follow {{: str.format's escaped braces ({{"nodes": []}}, {{ }}) stay as they are.
expression.name: variable.meta.scope.jinja

statement.comment: {% for doc in documents %}, {%- if x -%}.
statement.name: meta.scope.jinja.tag
